findings.claim_text: (3) modifying computer data without authorisation (e.g. installing malware)
findings.issue: The lesson describes CMA offence 3 as 'modifying computer data without authorisation'. The original 1990 Act section 3 heading was 'Unauthorised modification of computer material', but the Police and Justice Act 2006 replaced it with 'Unauthorised acts with intent to impair, or with recklessness as to impairing, operation of computer, etc.' — a broader formulation. The lesson uses the original pre-2006 wording. At GCSE level this is the conventional simplified teaching description used across OCR resources, so it is not materially misleading but is technically the superseded wording.
findings.correct_version: The current CMA section 3 offence is 'Unauthorised acts with intent to impair the operation of a computer' (amended by Police and Justice Act 2006). For GCSE purposes describing it as 'modifying computer material without authorisation' is an accepted simplification. The example '(e.g. installing malware)' is accurate — DoS attacks and malware installation both fall under section 3.

findings.claim_text: Bluetooth connects devices at short range (typically up to 10 metres) and is used for peripherals and file transfer.
findings.issue: Bluetooth range varies widely by power class. Class 1 devices reach approximately 100 m, Class 2 approximately 10 m, Class 3 approximately 1 m. Typical consumer devices (audio, wearables) operate at 10–30 m. Stating 'up to 10 metres' as the typical range is an understatement that could mislead students about modern Bluetooth capability. It describes only Class 2/3 devices and not Class 1 or Bluetooth 5.0+ which extends range further.
findings.correct_version: Bluetooth connects devices wirelessly at short to medium range — typically 10–100 metres depending on device class and implementation. Class 2 consumer devices (the most common, used in headphones and keyboards) reach approximately 10–30 metres. Class 1 devices can reach up to 100 metres.
